title: Miketz: at the end of two years (Genesis 41:1, 14)
hook: the waiting ends in a day; Joseph is shaved and brought out

segments.voice: Yesterday, a prisoner who noticed two sad faces. Your line was notice the sad face. Did you ask someone how they really were? Today, a new portion. Day two hundred six.

Waiting for the call back after the interview. Waiting for the test results. Waiting for the visa, the transplant list, the baby. Days that feel exactly like the day before. When Joseph read the cupbearer's dream, he asked him one thing: when you're free, remember me, and mention me to Pharaoh. The cupbearer was freed three days later. And the Torah says, with brutal simplicity, that he did not remember Joseph. He forgot him. The days go on in the dungeon. This portion is called Miketz, at the end. Today: at the end of two years.
screen: `WAITING FOR THE CALL.` → `REMEMBER ME.` → `HE FORGOT HIM.`

segments.voice: The portion opens, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "And it came to pass at the end of two full years, that Pharaoh dreamed." Two full years. Seven hundred mornings, give or take, in a prison, after hope had come so close. The rabbis asked why two years. An old midrash, which Rashi brings, gives a hard answer: Joseph put his trust in the cupbearer, asking him twice to remember him, and so he waited two more years. Other teachers push back, gently: asking for help isn't wrong. The Torah itself doesn't say why. It only counts the time. And then, everything changes in a single day. Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows eaten by seven thin ones, and nobody in Egypt can explain it. The cupbearer suddenly remembers. Oh. I have to confess something today. There was a young Hebrew in prison. Pharaoh sends for Joseph, and look how fast the verbs move: "they brought him hastily out of the dungeon." He shaves. He changes his clothes. He walks in before Pharaoh. Morning in a pit, afternoon in a palace. There's a Jewish saying, still loved today: God's help comes in the blink of an eye. It isn't a promise about when. Joseph waited two full years, and nobody told him the date. But it's a reminder that long waiting and sudden change live side by side. The same prisoner who was forgotten is the one they're running to fetch. Miketz, at the end, means that endings come, and sometimes all at once.
screen: `AT THE END OF TWO FULL YEARS.` · `WHY TWO YEARS?` · `BROUGHT HASTILY OUT OF THE DUNGEON.` · `HELP IN THE BLINK OF AN EYE.` · then, large: `IT ENDS SUDDENLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay ready for a sudden change. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've been waiting on for a long time. Feel the weight of the waiting, honestly. Then picture Joseph, the morning they came running: he shaved, he changed his clothes, he was ready. What would being ready look like for you? One small thing you could keep in order, so that if the door opens, you can walk through. The bell holds the time.
Miketz. At the end: the portion that opens after two full years of waiting, and brings Joseph out of the dungeon in a single day.
Your line: it ends suddenly. Today, while you wait on something, do one thing to be ready for the day it changes. Day two hundred six.

screen: `DAY 206 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: IT IS NOT IN ME.`

howItsDone: Miketz is read in synagogues in early winter, and Jews often repeat the saying that God's help comes in the blink of an eye, yeshuat Hashem k'heref ayin, in hard times.

original.note: Hebrew: at the end. the first word of the portion: at the end of two full years.

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph got a lucky break.
what it means: after two long years, the waiting ended all at once.
what a scholar hears: Rashi (from Genesis Rabbah 89:3) says Joseph waited two more years for relying on the cupbearer; other commentators defend his asking.
